title: Older Americans Month Community BINGO Challenge
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content: Every May, Older Americans Month recognizes the contributions of older adults, highlights aging trends, and reaffirms commitments to serve our older community members. The 2026 theme is “Champion Your Health”.Throughout the month of May, Oxford Seniors, Age-Friendly Oxford, and the Coalition for a Healthy Community, Oxford Area are partnering to highlight and offer programming focused on promoting physical, mental, and emotional health and well-being at all ages.You can participate by playing “Community BINGO” with us! It’s as easy as 1, 2, 3!1) Print your own or pick up a Community Bingo card at any of the following locations:Oxford Seniors, 922 Tollgate Dr., OxfordOxford Lane Library, 441 S. Locust St.The Knolls of Oxford, Clubhouse or Front DeskScripps Gerontology Center, 396 Upham Hall, on campus2) Every time you do something listed on the card, mark it off. The goal is to get “BINGO” as many times as possible. A “BINGO” is marking off any 5 squares in a straight line – either vertically, horizontally, or diagonally.3) Bring your completed BINGO card to the Intergenerational BINGO Party on Sun. May 31 from 3:00 – 5:00 p.m. at Oxford Seniors for prizes, snacks, and FUN! A PDF version of the BINGO card is attached to this message if you'd like to print one at home.

title: Summer Reading Tips to Prevent Learning Loss
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
NOTES 

FROM 

TITLE 

TALK 

NOTES FROM TITLE TALK

As we approach the end of the school year, we want to address the issue of “Summer Slide”. Younger students are at greater risk of losing skills learned throughout the school year because they are at a crucial stage of development. According to Scholastic, “Summer Slide” has been a topic of research since at least 1996. There are many ways to keep this from happening to your student, without making summer reading boring. Some examples of this: Keep books in your students’ hands by visiting the library or the Bookmobile. (You will need a library card.) Link to Lane LibraryE-books can be found for free with your library card at HooplaDigital.com Look for a “Little Free Library” in your neighborhood. One can be found outside your elementary school. Activities: Create a cozy reading space for your student with lights, comfy pillows, and stuffed animals to read to.Go camping with your student in your living room with a blanket fort, flashlight, and a good book.Participate in a summer reading bingo challenge. Here is one you may like from Scholastic! Summer Reading BingoMost importantly, please read with your child over the summer! YOU are the best teacher for your child!

summary: As the school year ends, families are encouraged to prevent "summer slide" (learning loss over summer break) by keeping students reading. Resources include **Lane Library**, the Bookmobile (library card needed), free e-books at **HooplaDigital.com**, and Little Free Libraries at elementary schools. Activity ideas include creating cozy reading spaces, building blanket forts for reading adventures, and participating in **[Scholastic's Summer Reading Bingo](https://www.scholastic.com/parents/books-and-reading/raise-a-reader-blog/summer-reading-bingo.html)**. Parents are reminded they are their child's best teacher.

title: Tips for Improving Student Reading Comprehension
source_title: Marshall E-News | Smore Newsletters for Education

blocks.content:
NOTES 

FROM 

TITLE 

TALK 

NOTES FROM TITLE TALK

Does your student understand what they are reading? A reader needs to understand what they are reading; simply reading the words is not enough. A good way to know if your student is understanding what they are reading is by asking questions. Questions about the story elements (characters, setting, events, etc.) let you know if your student is comprehending the text. Some questions you may want to ask:Who is the main character? Where does the story take place? (Setting: place and time)What is the problem? How was the problem solved?Activities: Ask your student to retell the story. Have your student draw a picture of the story. In Reading Corner, we are using the UFLI curriculum. Here is a parent resource for you to look at!Parent reading help K-3If you need help with any of these activities, please reach out to your student’s Reading Corner teacher.

summary: Parents can help assess reading comprehension by asking questions about story elements like characters, setting, and plot. **Suggested activities**: have students retell the story or draw pictures about what they read. The Reading Corner program uses the **UFLI curriculum** and offers a [parent resource guide](Parent reading help K-3). Contact your student's Reading Corner teacher for additional support.
